title: AI Exit Tickets That Grade Themselves (Without Extra Work)
author: Teaching With Intelligence
summary: Teachers spend time administering exit tickets but rarely use the resulting data. This workflow automates analysis: a Google Form captures student responses, which auto-sync to a sheet connected to Claude/GPT through Make or Zapier. The AI sorts responses by readiness level and emails summaries grouped by period, so actionable insights land in your inbox before you leave campus. The three-minute routine projects a QR code during independent practice, students submit silently, and AI automation handles the sorting while students pack up. Teachers spend 90 seconds filing insights: moving parent-friendly summaries into canned email responses, adding student names to an Interventions database for follow-up, and forwarding trend notes to co-teachers. Implementation requires Google Form (free), Make/Zapier ($10–15/month for basic automation), and either Claude or GPT API access. The prompt provided instructs AI to identify three major patterns, flag students needing follow-up, and draft parent summaries. Templates for the form, automation recipe, and exact prompt are available on request. This workflow transforms exit tickets from a compliance chore into formative assessment with accountability. Instead of 150 responses sitting unreviewed, teachers get structured evidence grouped by period and readiness level, enabling immediate small-group interventions and targeted reteaching before the next lesson.
points: Exit tickets fail because teachers lack time to manually sort 150 responses. Automation surfaces trends by period and readiness level in < 3 minutes of teacher effort.
Pair the AI summary with a data table that flags students needing follow-up by period, enabling teachers to pre-identify who to pull first for small-group reteaching.
Use the AI's parent-friendly summary as a template for class updates, turning raw data into communication that shows families what students are learning and where support is needed.
The QR code + shortlink workflow takes no longer than a verbal exit ticket but guarantees every student responds and every response gets analyzed. Silence during submission reduces off-task behavior.
Store summaries and intervention data in a persistent database (Notion, Airtable, Excel) so teachers spot repeat patterns across weeks and adjust instruction based on cumulative evidence.
quotes: Kids need 10–15 seconds of context or they give one-word answers.
Teachers don't have time to manually sort 150 responses.
The data never reaches the people who could help: co-teachers, SPED team, admin.
Make/Zapier sees the new line, feeds it to your large-language-model prompt, and emails you a summary with links grouped by readiness level.
The three-minute routine projects a QR code as soon as independent practice winds down.
While they pack up, you tap the Google Form response count to make sure every name is green.
